Abstract.AbstractText: Fibrocytes are circulating cells that have fibroblast properties. They are produced by the bone marrow stroma, and they move from the blood to injured organs using multiple chemokine pathways. They exhibit marked functional and phenotypic plasticity in response to the local tissue microenvironment to ensure a pro-inflammatory or a more resolving phenotype. They can adopt immune cell properties and modulate conventional immune cell functions. Although their exact function is not always clear, they have emerged as key effector cells in several fibrotic diseases like keloid, scleroderma, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Recently, evidence suggested that fibrocytes could contribute to bronchial obstructive diseases like asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). In this review, we summarize the reported roles of fibrocytes and their pathfinding into the lung in the context of asthma and COPD. We give an overview of the different roles played by fibrocytes and discuss their possible contributions to these obstructive diseases.
